title: Argentina threatens oil firms with sanctions as Falkland Islands dispute intensifies
summary:
Argentina threatens oil firms with sanctions as Falkland Islands dispute intensifies

Argentina has threatened sanctions on oil firms that seek to drill around the Falkland Islands as it continues to up the pressure on the British Overseas Territory.

The country's far-right president Javier Milei said in a national address that the "winds of change" favoured Argentina's claim to the islands, which they refer to as Las Malvinas.

He cited a threat by US President Donald Trump to change his country's position on the islands over the UK's lack of support for the war on Iran.

“Recently, President Trump declared that the US is re-evaluating its historic position in relation to the Malvinas,” said Milei.

He said that the UK was on "a path of decline" as a result of immigration.

"Argentina’s future, however, is flourishing and will prevail," Milei said.

title: Witkoff and Kushner to visit Russia and Ukraine at weekend, says Tass
summary:
Witkoff and Kushner to visit Russia and Ukraine at weekend, says Tass

US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Russia and Ukraine on Saturday and Sunday, Russian news agency Tass reported, citing a source.

There was no immediate confirmation. Witkoff and Kushner last visited Moscow in January, when they held four hours of late-night talks with President Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin, Reuters reported.

The two men are also US President Donald Trump's lead negotiators on Gaza and the war on Iran. 

If the visit takes place it will be their first to Kyiv. “The Russians don't want them to visit Kyiv and are trying to make them change the plan,” the source told the Russian news agency.

The last US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine took place in February, shortly before the United States and Israel launched their war on Iran.

title: ‘There was blood everywhere’: Survivors recount US strike on wedding in Iran
summary:
‘There was blood everywhere’: Survivors recount US strike on wedding in Iran

Submitted by MEE correspondent on Fri, 09/04/2026 - 10:28
Witnesses describe chaos and devastation as a family celebration instantly turned into a night of mourning
A medic runs an ultrasound on an injured child following an overnight strike in Kuhestak, southern Iran, on 2 September 2026 (Morteza Akhondi/Tasnim News/AFP)
Off

Maryam and Ziaeddin were meant to spend the most memorable night of their lives surrounded by their loved ones. They had no idea that their wedding would become the darkest moment of their lives and one of the most painful nights of the war for Iranians.

On the evening of Tuesday 1 September, around 350 people gathered in Kuhestak, in Sirik county, on the east coast of Iran’s Hormozgan province, for the wedding of Maryam Mallahi and Ziaeddin.

In keeping with local tradition, the celebration was held in two houses: the men gathered at a relative’s home, while the women waited at the bride’s family home. Coloured lights had been put up, the guests wore traditional clothing, and everyone was waiting for the bride and groom to arrive.

At around 9pm, as the United States launched a new wave of attacks across southern Iran, a series of explosions was heard in Kuhestak.

Initial reports indicated that a telecommunications tower and facilities near the pier had been hit. The tower stood less than 200 metres from the wedding venue. Moments later, a projectile struck the house where the women and children had gathered, tearing through its roof.

Majid, 41, was at the men’s gathering nearby. His wife and five-year-old child were both wounded.

“We were talking to some of the other guests when suddenly we heard a terrifying sound,” he told Middle East Eye. “At first, we thought it was an earthquake. We panicked and ran outside.

“We rushed towards the bride’s house and saw smoke and fire everywhere. I pulled my wife and my five-year-old child from beneath the rubble. Screams were coming from every direction. There was blood everywhere, and everyone was desperately trying to help the wounded.”

Ali Mallahi, the bride’s father and the owner of the house, said he heard a second and then a third explosion and realised the sounds appeared to be coming from the direction of his home.

‘Everyone was screaming. Everyone was calling for help. Nobody knew what had happened. I was trapped beneath the rubble’

– Mina, wedding guest

“The first explosion completely destroyed the single-storey house and left it uninhabitable,” he said. “The second struck the courtyard, damaging a car and other parts of the property. The house is not a home any more. It is gone.”

One of the projectiles pierced the roof and left a crater about 1.5 metres deep in the floor of one of the rooms, according to a news report.

Mina, one of the guests, was among the women trapped inside. She was later taken to Abolfazl Hospital in the nearby city of Minab.

“We were eating ice cream,” she told MEE. “You know, the weather is still very hot in Hormozgan at this time of year. We were waiting for the bride and groom to arrive when suddenly we heard a terrifying explosion somewhere near the house.”

She said a second explosion struck the house soon afterwards and tore a hole through the roof.

“Bricks and pieces of the ceiling and walls suddenly came down on us,” she said. “Everyone was screaming. Everyone was calling for help. Nobody knew what had happened. I was trapped beneath the rubble. I was lucky to survive.”

Zahra, 19, was another of those wounded.

“Every carpet in the house was stained with blood,” she told MEE. “The shoes, the serving dishes and the lights they had put up for the wedding all had blood on them.”

Pulling survivors from the rubble

Residents began searching for survivors before emergency teams reached the house.

A Red Crescent worker who arrived with his colleagues minutes after the attack said those who had escaped the building and people from surrounding homes were already trying to free the injured.

“People who had been inside the building, as well as others who had seen the attack from outside, were already trying to pull the wounded and survivors from beneath the rubble,” the rescuer, who asked not to be named, told MEE.

‘Amir Mohammad was supposed to start preschool in just a few days... Now his parents have to attend his funeral. The grief is unbearable’

– Fatemeh, wedding guest

“They were so terrified that we had to spend some of our time and energy calming them down. Of course they were terrified. This was a real tragedy. It took only a few moments for their wedding to turn into mourning.”

Fifteen ambulances were sent to the area. Most were taken to hospitals in Sirik and Minab, with several of the most seriously wounded admitted directly to intensive care.

Iranian officials initially reported two deaths and about 50 injuries. The death toll later rose to four: 50-year-old Zarkhatoun Taheri, 43-year-old Kolsoum Mallahi-Nezhadnia, 16-year-old Mohammad Mallahi and four-year-old Amir Mohammad Karimi.

On Thursday, 22-year-old Asieh Molaeinejad died in hospital, bringing the death toll to five.

A total of 68 people were wounded, according to provincial authorities. Hormozgan’s emergency services said 19 of them were children under the age of 10.

Fatemeh, another guest who suffered relatively minor injuries, knew Amir Mohammad and his family.

“Amir Mohammad was supposed to start preschool in just a few days, when the new school year began,” she told MEE. “Now his parents have to attend his funeral. The grief is unbearable.”

Washington 'investigating' attack

It is still unclear exactly what kind of weapon hit the house. Some witnesses interviewed by MEE believed it was a missile, while others spoke of drones. No official account has yet established precisely how the attack was carried out.

Razieh Alishvandi, the Iranian Red Crescent’s deputy for international and humanitarian affairs, described the incident as a projectile striking a residential home during a wedding.

Everyone interviewed by MEE said the building was entirely residential and that there were no military, security or intelligence facilities nearby.

The attack on Kuhestak was part of a broader wave of strikes across Hormozgan and other areas of southern Iran that night. Iranian officials reported attacks or explosions in Bandar Abbas, Qeshm, Jask, Sirik, Konarak and Chabahar.

In Kuhestak, the telecommunications tower, parts of the pier and electricity and communications infrastructure were also damaged. Mobile phone and internet services were temporarily cut in Kuhestak and the nearby village of Mishi.

For residents of Hormozgan, the attack brought back memories of the strike on the Shajareh Tayyebeh girls’ school in Minab on 28 February that killed 156 people, most of them children, the first day of the US-Israeli attacks on Iran.

‘She had dreamed about this night for so long... Now her mental state is so fragile that we honestly do not know how she will cope with this tragedy’

– A friend of the bride

US officials have not said what the precise target in Kuhestak was.

US Central Command said the strikes that night targeted Iranian radar and communications facilities and maritime capabilities, adding that the US military does not target civilians. US Vice-President JD Vance later said Washington was investigating the incident.

Maryam and Ziaeddin survived because neither had reached the house when it was hit. The guests were still waiting for the young couple to arrive, but everyone killed or wounded was a relative, friend or acquaintance of theirs.

A friend of Maryam’s, who asked not to be named, said the bride was still in deep shock.

“Maryam is in a very bad state – very, very bad,” she told MEE. “She had dreamed about this night for so long. She wanted to celebrate the beginning of her married life with her family and friends. Now her mental state is so fragile that we honestly do not know how she will cope with this tragedy.”

title: Two Alleged ‘TeamPCP’ Hackers Arrested in Australia
summary:
Authorities in Australia have arrested two men believed to be members of TeamPCP, a prolific cybercrime and data extortion group blamed for perpetrating the longest running spree of software supply chain attacks ever.

In a statement released today, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) said two unnamed suspects from Western Australia, aged 21 and 23, were arrested in connection with a "sophisticated cybercrime syndicate that allegedly created malicious open-source software to rob thousands of global businesses."

The AFP did not name the defendants, but KrebsOnSecurity learned the 21-year-old suspect's real identity in June, and has been communicating with him ever since. This story includes interviews with TeamPCP's self-described spokesperson, and examines clues left behind by the TeamPCP leader that likely led to his undoing.

title: AI Coding Agents Are Installing Unknown/Untrusted Code on Corporate Networks
summary:
We cannot forget that AI coding agents are not yet trustworthy:

Researchers at a stealth startup in Israel scanned 6,214 live domains belonging to defense contractors, Fortune 500, and Big Tech companies. Of the 8,265 llms.txt and llms-full.txt files they found (many sites hosted both an llms.txt and an llms-full.txt file), 120 of them, each on a different site, pointed to one or more code packages or domain names that weren’t registered. To test what happens when an AI agent processes such files, the researchers registered a handful of the unclaimed names and hosted packages that caused any machine executing them to reach out to their server. Within an hour, the researchers received a phone-home response from a Fortune 500 company. Over time, they got a few dozen more, some from more Fortune 500 companies and others from startups. Their beacon also recorded the chain of parent processes that spawned each install, ultimately revealing that coding agents, including Claude, OpenAI’s Codex, and Nous Research’s Hermes, were involved. Anthropic, OpenAI, and Nous Research did not respond to requests for comment by the time of publication...

title: Israeli charged for alleged role in hostile foreign influence campaign
summary:
Israeli charged for alleged role in hostile foreign influence campaign

Israeli authorities have indicted an Israeli citizen on security offenses for allegedly carrying out activities on behalf of foreign intelligence operatives targeting Israel, the Shin Bet security service and police said on Friday.

The man was arrested by the Shin Bet and police and questioned on suspicion of being recruited by foreign intelligence operatives, Haaretz reported.

The authorities say the investigation found that he had been involved in a foreign influence operation. An indictment and a request to keep him in custody until the end of legal proceedings were filed after the investigation concluded.

The Israeli citizen was arrested a month ago after landing at Ben Gurion Airport and barred from meeting with his attorney for 20 days.

title: World food prices at highest since 2022, says UN
summary:
World food prices at highest since 2022, says UN

World food prices rose in August to their highest since late 2022, impacted partly by the war on Iran, the United Nations' Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) said on Friday.

Extreme heat and drought in Europe, the threat of a severe El Nino weather pattern and trade upheaval caused by the Ukraine and Iran wars have unsettled agricultural markets, pushing grain prices to three-year highs and sugar to a one-year peak, the agency said.

The FAO Food Price Index, which tracks monthly changes in a basket of internationally traded food commodities, averaged 133.3 points in August, up from July's revised reading of 130.8.

That was the highest score since November 2022, though nearly 17 percent below a record peak from March 2022, after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Reuters reported.

Escalating attacks in the Black Sea have curtailed grain shipments from Russia and Ukraine, while the war on Iran is still straining flows of fertiliser for crops.

title: How UK 'wudu-gate' avoids naming the real culprit for the climate crisis
summary:
How UK 'wudu-gate' avoids naming the real culprit for the climate crisis

Submitted by Khadijah Elshayyal on Wed, 09/02/2026 - 20:24
Our mosque leaders must urgently address the dangers of AI usage, which is heating the planet and further demonising Muslim communities
A fountain in the Islamic garden of Cambridge Central Mosque is pictured in 2021 (AFP)
On

In mid-August, as the UK grappled with its fourth heatwave of the year, news headlines decried the water regulator’s allegedly wasteful use of public funds in its campaign advising Muslims to use less water for wudu (an ablution or cleansing ritual before prayer), and Asians to reduce water usage when washing rice. 

It turns out that ferocious heatwaves offer up valuable opportunities for flagging media outlets on slow news days. 

As is the norm with other manufactured hysterias, “wudu-gate” recycled a years-old initiative to viral effect, through the use of dramatic headlines, head-turning stock images and hyperbolic openers. 

Language and visuals are powerful tools wielded by the media in shaping and stoking public opinion. When the Telegraph uses phrases like “religious and cultural practices” to inform us that “Asian and Muslim communities have been told to wash their rice and feet less” in a “bizarre” water-saving push, it marks these groups out as separatist offenders, thoughtlessly and selfishly indulging at the expense of others during a time of national crisis. 

It is unsurprising, then, that in the current climate of rising Islamophobia, this news (non-)story was met with weary suspicion from many, as yet another attempt by the media to frame Muslims as the perpetrators of the UK’s drought. 

Perhaps it could be argued that the water regulator’s recent community outreach campaign, in collaboration with the Cambridge Central Mosque and funded under its broader “water efficiency in faith and diverse communities” project, was DEI overkill - but it was hardly front-page news. 

Yet from moral panics about halal meat, to fear-mongering about mega-mosques, our media outlets are primed to magnify moments like these. They delight in creating otherising caricatures out of minoritised communities. 

Theatrics and deflection

Just days after having hounded Jason Arday to death, the critics of “woke nonsense” moved on to a new target. We were, predictably, treated to images of Muslim feet in the sink, along with headlines slamming the waste of £270,000 ($364,000) of taxpayers’ money - thus linking a broader project that worked with a wide range of communities across the country, directly and primarily with Muslims and their implied thoughtless, wasteful lifestyles. 

Here we are enduring hosepipe bans, while the Muslims are sloshing their feet about in the sink with abandon five times a day! It is a theatrical performance, of course - because at its core, it is a deflection from the real culprit. 

It is a deflection from the extortionate use of AI, and the government’s active investment in its infrastructural growth, amid plans to increase the number of data centres in the UK - facilities that have been described as “data heat islands”, driving up surrounding temperatures by an average of 2C. 

Wudu-gate is simply another panel in an interminable comic strip, which just like AI, seems destined to continue regenerating warped permutations of itself

The London Assembly recently released a stark report noting that the construction of data centres will significantly delay the construction of housing, a crisis that has engulfed the city for years. 

The Save Brick Lane campaign has ardently protested against the construction of a data centre on the site of the iconic Truman Brewery, and as a councillor for Tower Hamlets reminded us, there are more than 30,000 people waiting for social housing, which will be further delayed by the construction of this data centre. 

If the environmental costs of AI and related infrastructure do not concern our communities, we can examine how generative AI in particular is increasing Islamophobia globally. 

Think back to the 2024 riots in the UK, where AI and algorithms played a violent role in orchestrating hate towards Muslims and other racialised groups, as social media sites like X (formerly Twitter) amplified misinformation targeting Muslim and immigrant communities.

If that’s not enough, we can look at how autonomous weapons were used indiscriminately in Gaza, or how generative AI is currently being used by Israeli politicians to dehumanise Palestinians and legitimise the occupation. 

The evidence against the use of AI is enormous, and just these two examples show the urgent need for leadership by mosques on this matter. As noble as it is to focus on the conservation of water in wudu, mosques should also address the more pressing issue of AI usage in our communities. 

Dizzying political ramifications

We need our mosques to address the unethical uses and practices of AI, from the environmental consequences to the dizzying political ramifications that are driving unprecedented levels of Islamophobia. Muslim leadership is desperately needed to resist the tentacles of AI.

At a time when Muslim institutions are facing intense and unforgiving public scrutiny, it is understandable that many will welcome opportunities to partner with public agencies and local governments for good causes. 

In this regard, campaigns on reducing water wastage are low-hanging fruit - a photogenic display of active citizenship, the spirit of which is perfectly aligned with Islamic injunctions condemning wastage and mandating responsible use of resources. What’s not to love? 

For many British Muslims, the UK has become a hostile home
Read More »

In fact, many Muslim organisations and mosques have been running no-waste wudu campaigns for years, including by installing auto-shut taps and raising awareness among their congregations. For mosque administrations that operate in a climate of suspicion and demonisation, it is an easy and non-divisive cause to sign up to; a great way to engender and demonstrate good citizenship and positive messaging about their beleaguered communities. 

But as others have noted, viewed in context, this civic participation renders Muslims agents of responsibilisation, and absolves politicians and media outlets alike from accountability for structural inequalities and injustices. 

Over the past few days, several Muslim civic voices have registered their objection to wudu-gate, recognising the cynical deflection that is embedded in its hyperbole.

But if Muslim institutions and leadership have learned anything from the past 25 years of dog-whistle Islamophobia, they will know that conscientious civic engagement in this moment should go further than simply calling out prejudice. 

Not only should we seek to redirect our attention towards properly holding our political and media classes to account, we would also do well to engage in a timely introspection and interrogate the extent of our own complicity with the harmful aspects of AI infrastructure and AI-creep in our everyday lives.

We need our mosques and leadership to become much more serious about environmental degradation and its intersection with other structural harms

In recent years, the uncritical use of generative AI has become ubiquitous in our community spaces with remarkable ease. We have seen our institutions reach for AI tools to generate text for khutbas, with embarrassing repercussions, potentially undermining trust in religious leadership.

Imagery and publicity for religious and social events as well as material for teaching and learning all routinely rely on AI generated text and visuals, to the point that notions of ‘AI-inevitability’ have almost become justifications for a growing passive reliance.

The unreflexive use of this technology poses serious ethical questions which can have lasting impacts, not only on our sense of who we are, but also on our safety and security, and that of other communities across the world. 

Returning to the question of how much water to use for rice-washing and wudu, by all means let us stick to two rinses and one litre. But public campaigns, and the outcries that thrive on misrepresenting them, can tell us far more about a nation’s political climate than they can about the state of its kitchen and bathroom sinks. 

The environment is inherently political. While the increasingly stark impacts of our overheating planet envelop our daily realities, the nativist populism that dominates our political discourse routinely holds up Muslims and other minoritised groups as scapegoats and sacrificial lambs, aiming to obscure the exposure of political and corporate corruption and incompetence. 

Wudu-gate is simply another panel in an interminable comic strip, which just like AI, seems destined to continue regenerating warped permutations of itself until its subjects - Muslim communities - develop the resolve to proactively name structural harms, and interrogate and address their potential complicity in them. 

We need our mosques and leadership to become much more serious about environmental degradation and its intersection with other structural harms.
